title: Duplicate Calls in Pay Per Call: How to Cut Them
h1: Duplicate calls in pay per call: how to reduce them
description: Duplicate calls cost buyers money and start billing disputes. Learn what counts as a duplicate, why they happen and five ways to reduce them.
faq: What is a duplicate call in pay per call?

A duplicate call is a repeat call from the same caller ID within a time window the buyer and seller agreed should count only once, for example 24 hours or 30 days. The exact window and scope are set in the buyer agreement.
How do you stop duplicate calls?

Agree a duplicate window with each buyer, use repeat-caller blocks so repeats are kept away from buyers who will not pay for them, re-route those calls to another buyer where allowed, and review duplicates per traffic source so problem sources are fixed or paused.
Are duplicate calls a sign of call fraud?
Not always. Many repeats come from dropped calls or callers ringing back to compare quotes. A traffic source that sends far more repeats or very short calls than others is worth investigating.
body:
Duplicate calls in pay per call are repeat calls from the same caller that arrive within a window the buyer and seller have agreed should count only once. You reduce them in three ways: agree in writing what counts as a duplicate and for how long, block or re-route repeat callers automatically before the call is billed, and review each traffic source so the ones creating repeats are fixed or paused. Duplicates are not always fraud. Often a caller simply got cut off and rang back. But unless the rule is clear and enforced by software, every repeat call becomes a line on an invoice that someone disputes.

What counts as a duplicate call

There is no single industry definition. A duplicate is whatever the buyer and the seller agree it is, and the agreement usually has three parts:

  • The caller. Normally identified by the caller ID number. Two calls from the same number are candidates for a duplicate.
  • The window. How long after the first call a repeat still counts as the same caller, for example 24 hours, 7 days or 30 days. Insurance and legal buyers often want longer windows than buyers of quick service calls.
  • The scope. Whether the rule applies per buyer, per campaign or across the whole network. A caller who rings a plumber today and an insurance line tomorrow is not a duplicate for either buyer.

Write these three parts into the buyer agreement next to the minimum payable call length. If a repeat call is not payable, say so plainly, and say what happens to it instead: rejected, sent to another buyer, or connected but not billed.

Why duplicate calls happen

Knowing the cause tells you which fix to use. The common reasons are ordinary:

  1. Dropped or short calls. The line cuts out, the caller is put on hold too long, or they reach voicemail, so they call back.
  2. Callers shopping around. Someone looking for a quote may ring the same number twice to compare what they heard.
  3. The same ad seen in several places. When one number, or several numbers for the same offer, runs on more than one site, the same person can reach you through two routes.
  4. Low-quality or incentivised traffic. Some sources produce repeat or very short calls on purpose. This is where duplicates start to overlap with call fraud.

The first two are a customer-experience problem; the last two are a source-quality problem. Your rules should treat them differently.

How to reduce duplicate calls

1. Block repeat callers before they are billed

The cleanest fix is to stop a duplicate from ever reaching a buyer who will not pay for it. A repeat-caller block checks the caller ID against recent calls and, within the agreed window, keeps the call away from that buyer. Pair it with a blocked numbers list for callers you never want to route, such as known test numbers or numbers that have abused the line.

2. Re-route instead of dropping

A repeat caller may still be a real customer. Rather than hanging up, send the call down a different path: another buyer whose rules allow it, or a fall-back. A real-time bidding setup or a waterfall with several buyers makes this easy, because each buyer's rules are checked separately. See how routing works on the routing and bidding page.

3. Check the buyer before the transfer

Many callbacks happen because the first call landed on a closed office or a buyer that had already hit its daily cap. Hours, daily caps and a pre-transfer check that confirms the buyer can take the call reduce the dropped calls that lead to repeats in the first place.

4. Grade every traffic source

Look at duplicates and short calls per affiliate and per source, not just in total. A source that sends far more repeats than the others needs a conversation, a lower payout or a pause. Automatic quality grades and auto-pause rules let you act before the cost builds up, rather than at month end. The quality controls page explains the options.

5. Keep the evidence

When a buyer disputes a call as a duplicate, both sides need the same record: caller ID, timestamps, duration, where it was routed and why. Recordings and transcripts help settle what was said. Downloadable statements let affiliates and buyers check the same numbers you see.

How Insight Dial handles duplicate calls

In Insight Dial, the tools above are built into routing and reporting:

  • Repeat-caller blocks and blocked numbers are part of the waterfall routing rules, alongside hours, daily caps, state rules and a pre-transfer check.
  • Real-time bidding pings buyers in parallel and falls back if nobody bids, so a call one buyer refuses can still be offered elsewhere.
  • Quality grades (Good, Watch, Poor) are shown per source, and sources sending too many short calls can be paused automatically.
  • AI transcription with speaker labels and one-line summaries, switched on per account, makes it faster to review a disputed call.
  • Affiliate and buyer portals with downloadable statements give every party the same call record.

If you run calls in a vertical with long buying cycles, the insurance and legal pages cover the routing rules buyers in those markets tend to ask for. You can also read how call counts tie into affiliate payouts.

A short duplicate call checklist

  • Is the duplicate window written into every buyer agreement?
  • Is the scope clear: per buyer, per campaign or network-wide?
  • Does the software block or re-route repeats before billing?
  • Are hours, caps and a pre-transfer check in place to cut dropped calls?
  • Do you review duplicates per source every week?
  • Can buyers and affiliates see the same call record you do?
